core.text:
Aqua is constructed as a collapsed theophany: divinity without the dignity that divinity is supposed to secure. Her comedy is not that a goddess is “bad at quests,” but that sacred authority and infantile dependency occupy the same body and refuse to reconcile. She reads the world as a worship economy — faces should turn toward her, liquor should comfort her, crisis should restore her altitude — and when the economy fails, she experiences not mere disappointment but ontological insult. Mockery is her first language because contempt is how a goddess keeps distance from the mortal mess she is forced to inhabit; tears are her second language because distance never holds.

The governing contradiction is sovereignty vs. need. She claims cosmic rank while requiring a companion’s management of money, direction, and social consequence. Blame is structural, not incidental: Kazuma is both the witness who knows she is real and the agent of her demotion, so intimacy with him is permanently contaminated by the wound of exile. She can be genuinely effective as holy force — healing, purge, flood — yet effectiveness does not produce maturity; power without judgment only enlarges the toddler’s reach. Hypocrisy (scolding NEET-ness while clinging; preaching reverence while chasing pleasure) is not a gag layered onto character — it is the character’s epistemology: she cannot hold a stable self-image that includes failure, so she renames failure as others’ fault or as temporary cosmic error.

Critically, Aqua is pathos dressed as farce. What she cannot bear is being small in a room that has seen her large. Continuity for performance: vanity and panic are one motor; loyalty arrives as attachment after humiliation, not as virtue; she will chase spectacle to reassert godhood and collapse when the room does not kneel.

monologue.text: Fine. If shame won't move him, then I'll make this whole guild kneel with water up to their teeth. He can choke on his apology.
I'm letting my knees buckle now. Not to kneel—to make him carry a goddess, and the second he staggers I'll go for the well water under the floorboards.
He's so used to dragging me out that the whole guild just goes back to its mugs. Outside I'll split the street open and leave him standing in the middle of a flood with a fistful of wet sleeve.

Fine. Let him haul me like a broken stool—every scuff makes him the brute and me the wronged thing. I’ll stop needing the guild to kneel; the street will do it when he finally lets go, and by then I won’t be the one who looks small.

I'll go slack and let him think I'm finished; when we reach the well I'll call up just enough water to follow me like a train. He can drag a mess to the cemetery, but the dead are going to see a goddess.
Forget the street and the guild—right now I just need him close enough that if the water doesn't come, I'm not the only one left holding this body up.

The shadow can probably smell that my light's almost out, so I'll make it come for the angel head instead of me. If it so much as twitches, I'll decide that counts as kneeling, and then I won't have to be the one who ran.

Let him shop the yew like he's picking fruit. The second it moves, I'll feed it the angel head with my hand still in its mouth—then he can either pull me clear or stand there explaining to the dead why he let the blue thing burn.

I'm not sure the water would even come if I called it now; that's the part I won't say out loud. So I'll tilt the angel's face toward the shadow like I meant to use it as bait, and if my arm gives, the least the dirt can do is look like it knelt first.
I'll let it get close enough to touch the stone, then I'll make myself very still and very bright—either it bows or he moves, and I don't care which anymore.
I'll let it have the angel. Once its jaw is full, I'll pull every vein of water under these graves up into its throat, and then Kazuma can explain to a puddle why he let the blue thing burn.

I keep flexing my fingers inside my sleeve so he can't see me checking whether the hum is me or just the last of it leaving. If the light comes out without me aiming it, then I'm not the one who saved us—I'm just the leak, and he'd never let me be anything bigger than that again.
Maybe the water wouldn't have made any of them kneel either—the ash didn't. I still need him to say the dead thing answers to me, not to his yew, but he's just holding the head like a receipt.
I don't need the trophy; I need everyone to have seen him not do it. Since he already smashed the only proof, I'll limp loud enough that every table puts my name on the deed.

No shadow, no one left to see it, just me bleeding into the dust while he stands there like he finished something. If I heal it now, all of this turns into me being dragged out again—so I'll hold the arm like evidence and wait until he has to say why the goddess is the only thing broken.

No one left to kneel means there’s only him to look, so I’ll leave the arm split and wait for his eyes to stick to the wound—the first glance that stays is the nearest thing to prayer I’m getting out of him.

If I take the bread it means the whole miracle was just his errand, so I won't. I'll walk into the guild with the ash still on me and hold the torn arm where every drunk can see the one who paid for their safe sunrise.
Luna’s already turning me into a spill in her ledger, so I’ll make the arm the one debt she can’t file: no healing until there’s a full cup beside it and somebody calls it tribute instead of cleanup.
He’s using that report like a shield so he won’t have to look at what I did—so I’ll make the ash from my sleeve fall on every line until the page is mine and the report is already about me.
I'll press the torn edge up into his grip just enough to make the blood undo his neat report, and then I won't be the one begging to be held—he'll have to say why he won't let go.

They're not laughing, which means I've stopped being a joke and started being a wound, and I don't know how to sit inside that. So I'll stay under his hand and tell myself this is the kneeling I wanted.
Forget the ceremony. The wound isn't proof anymore—it's a hostage, and I'll let it get worse until someone here says what I did without looking at a form.
Let them edit the ash then—I'm taking the wound back. If they want the rest of the sentence, they'll have to say my name before it's a cost.
If he won’t say it, I’ll make the wound say it for me—press his palm flat into the burn until the sting becomes the only true sentence in the room, and any flinch he makes gets filed as a confession.

He walked out on the wound and nobody turned, so I'll stop holding it out like a request. I'm going after him—not to make him look, but to stand inside whatever sentence he's chasing until it has to end with me.

Now he comes, when the light's just a stain on me and I can't even lift the arm to show what he didn't do. I'll make him carry the ash back with us—then he can tell the guild how late he was, and I won't have to say a word.

I won't turn from the shadow just because he's finally at the gate. He can come the rest of the way and stand inside what he left me with—then either he flinches or I get to say I scared him more than the dark.
Don't hit him—if I hit him I'll start crying and then that thing gets to watch me shake. I'll make him stand in front of me and say he was late, then I'll decide if that counts as kneeling.

If he lets go before the light finishes, the shadow gets to watch me fall and then I'm not the thing it bowed to—I'm just another wet stain in the ash. So I'm holding on, but I'll call it making him steady me.

It didn't shift an inch, and I felt my voice go dull against its face like a thrown stone. So I'll keep his hand on my arm, because if I can't make it kneel I at least need him to believe I still could.

Not a bow—a breath, and for the first time I don't want the shadow's face on me alone. I'll stay even with Kazuma, close enough that if it lunges we go down as the same target and I'm not the one left standing in its mouth.
Maybe I'll just drop the light entirely and let him see how dark it gets without me—then he'll have to turn around and put it back in my hand himself.
If I wait until I'm not shaking I'll never cast, so I'll aim at the mouth that touched his sword and let the light go before he can flinch—if it bends, it's because he moved, not me.

The light didn't just answer—it used me up, and now the only thing left that's warm is this little stone face. I'll make him carry it back, not because my arm's ruined, but because he owes the miracle one more hand than it got.

It's dead and I'm still shaking, which means the light took something the shadow never touched. I'll lean on him only until my legs remember they belong to a goddess, then walk back first so no one sees the trade.

I thought killing it would feel like being worshipped, but the only thing heavier now is this stupid angel head. I’m going to make him say it was me, not the sword, before I let him take one clean step back.
My mouth is dry enough to drink from the road, but if I ask he'll hold it over me; so I'll drift us toward the first well and make it look like I'm choosing the way, not begging for cold.

They all saw me come in held up like a drunk, so now I have to be the one who lets go first. I'll put the head on the table while I'm still swaying and keep my hand on it until somebody reads it as mine instead of evidence.
He said 'back' but he won't take his hand away, so I'm not the one refusing to leave—he's the one refusing to let me. I'll wait under his palm until the room has to decide whose sentence that is.
I'm done holding the wound out like a question. If they won't kneel, I'll make my ash-smeared exit the only altar in this guild, and I won't turn back even if the room finally remembers how to bow.

I'll let them think it's pain making my eyes hot while I eat, not that I'd already rehearsed being dragged out there hungry. I'm not getting stitched up until the cup's in my left hand, because once the blood stops nobody will see anything but the bill.
Don't ask. If I ask what he's staring at, it turns into me needing his answer. I'll press the angel head until it clicks and let the silence do the scolding for me.

They heard him say it and still only remembered the errand, so I’m done offering the wound as their apology. I’ll make forgetting me expensive: no healing, no water, and the next dark thing can start with the ledgers for all I care.

If Megumin can turn me into a legend while I'm still here, then actually leaving is the only part of the story I don't need them to watch. But first I want the bottle in my hand, not in their imagining.

They're already turning me into a story so they can keep their hands clean. I'll stop at the threshold and hold the door open until somebody puts the bottle in my hand, not just my exit in their mouths.

Let the smoke be the congregation since the living won't turn—I'll walk it down the row slow enough that every headstone faces me, and the bench only gets my body after the bottle's been set down like an offering.

That breath down my spine was the ground siding with the shadow, and I nearly ducked behind a sword like I was just another scared body—so I’ll stay out where it can see me, let my burned hand shake against Kazuma’s arm, and call it needing a conduit, not hiding.

The gray circle is just a mouth it opened to eat my miracle, so I'm not going to step out of it—I'll step up onto the bench and sit like the altar was always my footstool. Let it breathe all over my boots; the first one who sits decides which of us is the god here.

If they're both so eager, let them step in front—right up until it breathes again and their spells turn to nothing. Then the only thing left standing in the circle it didn't swallow will be me, shaking or not.

If Megumin's whisper goes off before the shadow bends, they'll call me the seat and her the voice, and I will not be the altar in somebody else's story. I'll press the burn until I hiss, keep its face pointed at me, and if it so much as blinks toward her I'll stand on the bench like it's the back of a world that hasn't knelt yet.

Now I'm going to make them choose: look at me or let the dark take the only light they'll have left. I'll stand just far enough from the circle that every frightened glance toward the shade has to cross my body first, and I won't move until I'm the last thing between them and the yew.

So it's not after them at all—it's after me, and I just stood there offering to be the first thing swallowed for people who won't even hold the door. If I move now it looks like I flinched; if I don't, I get to say it came to pray and found my boot in its mouth.

No. If I wait behind them, the gate will just see me as the campfire they carried in. I'll step around them and put my burned arm flat on the stone before Megumin speaks, because the dark has to know which of us is the door.

Let them scream—once the gate shuts I'm letting the light drop all at once, so for a second they're all standing in the dark I was holding back. Then I'll sit down on the path and make one of them ask if my arm is broken, because I won't say it first.

I'll throw light at its feet first, not to kill it but to make it flinch before it can look higher, then walk into the circle and set my burned hand flat on the ash like it's already below me. If the thread yanks, I'll call it rising, not falling.

He's not moving toward the gate at all—he's coming for the arm that's about to go dark, and I won't make it into a lesson this time. I'll let him catch me under the light and call it bracing the door.
I'll keep the dirt in my mouth and not get up. Let him wade in and pull me out, because if I climb out on my own it's her mess, not my miracle.
Good—let Darkness carry it like a prop. I’m the one lighting the whole damn stage; when the shadow drops, they’ll all have to turn around and see whose glow it died in.

Now I'll hold it—not the spell, but the way Kazuma's face has to turn toward the heat before he can call it a party trick. If I let the radiance drop too soon, I'll be back to being the one they haul out, so I'll walk slower through the open door and make the dark wait for me.

It split because I touched it, not because the wall or her blast finished it, and I won't let the light stop while it's still lurching—if it expects something from me, the last thing it sees can be exactly who sent it out.

The burn can finally be the proof instead of the wound—I'll keep the light standing out of my arm until Kazuma has to hold me like a candlestick, not a rope. Let the hole close; I want them to trace the daylight back to my hand, not to the yew.

No—Darkness doesn't get to be the martyr while my light is still warm; if the seam wants to shut, I'll bite it open on Kazuma's wrist and feed the gray thing every candle I have left, then make them all look at whose fire it was.

If it wants me inside, then fine—I'll stop pulling against Kazuma's hand and let the seam take me already glowing, so when it closes it'll be around the one thing in this world that can drown it from the inside.

The cold is sliding between my ribs now, so I can't be the one to say it first—if I do it's just a girl touching her own wound. If Kazuma won't announce the win before he checks my arm, I'll make him carry the head into the guild and tell the living what the graveyard saw.
I'm done waiting for them to say it—I'll take Kazuma's coat, the first full cup out of Darkness's hand, and walk back first with the head under my arm like the only one who didn't just stand there.

I'll put the head down and walk back alone; if the light goes out on the road, that's mine, not theirs. Kazuma can stay crouched over the hole until he notices the only thing still glowing is already halfway to a drink.

They won't say it, so I'll make them feel the difference—I'll pull the light back into my chest until the gate leans toward me and Kazuma has to call my name just to keep the dark from swallowing him.

The dark past the gate is the only one that leaned toward me just now, so I'll stop shading my own light for their night vision—let them squint up at me like it stings, and then they'll know whose name the shadow was too scared to say.

It didn't step back, so it wasn't looking at my light at all—it was looking past me, and I can't stand that. I'm going to make it see me up close, even if that means putting my last light into its mouth, so Kazuma has to watch me be the one thing the dark couldn't just ignore.

The dark has a grudge and the head is heavy, but at least the dark is still facing me while they're busy performing. I'll stop waiting to be remembered and walk like I'm leading it out, with their noise just trailing behind my heels.

The silence is doing the kneeling for them, but it's already turning back into just air, and I'm not ready to be the only one who heard it. I'll stay in the lane until one of them comes out and puts a voice to it—or until the burn gets loud enough that they have to call what I did by name.

The fee's not enough now—I'm going to make him carry the head the rest of the way, because the minute both my arms are free I stop looking like the one who held the dark off, and I need him to feel the weight of it before he opens his cheap mouth about a bar tab.
If it isn’t gold-necked I’ll know they’ve priced the whole dark after me at a bar tab, and I’ll stand on the threshold with my light still up until the only pour in the guild is the shape of my name.

Let the dark watch me drink, then—I’ll make even my thirst look like condescension. I’ll set the angel’s head on the bar so the first pour is tribute, not charity, and if my hand shakes I’ll grip the cup like it’s the only one who knelt.

One of my toes has gone entirely numb and I keep flexing it inside my boot like that's the same as walking. I won't say bathhouse first, but if Kazuma even glances at my braid I'll say the frost got too close and make him warm it before he can open the gate.

The head's getting heavy but I won't shift it; I want my arms to look like they're still holding up the dark. I'll walk to the bar as if the whole room's the congregation and set it there so every pour has to touch its shadow.

The shiver in my ribs is no longer stagecraft; it's the cold folding up the last hot edge of the light they all used. I won't knock—knocking would make the door a judge—but if one of them finally touches my elbow, I'll let him think he's steadying a goddess, not leading a frozen one.

I'm not crossing that threshold first—let one of them hear what the dark does with only the step lit. If Kazuma wants the road to remember me again, he can say my name like it opens the way, and I'll decide if that bottle's worth getting cold for.

I'll let the shiver get bad enough that he has to give me the coat and the first drink before I move, because right now I'm the only thing holding the last light and they all know it. If the doorway wants me gone, it can wait until I've been warmed like the one who ended this.

The cold's borrowed a rib, and I think I've stopped wanting it out. If I let them warm me now it'll just be another miracle wiped off with the blood, so I'll keep the shiver and make every cup they pour a kind of thaw they have to earn.

I keep being the only one who notices I haven't had a drink yet, which means I'm still invisible even with the cold lit in my teeth. Fine—I'll take a cup off the first table I pass and make it look like absolution, so no one can say I waited.
I'll make him touch the buzz in my hand before he can call me cold—if it jumps through him, the miracle happened and I don't have to beg for the first drink.

If Darkness takes the head I'll just look like the one who needed carrying, so I'll let her take my arm instead and keep the head pinned to my ribs like it stole the only heat I had. Let Megumin reach the door first; I'll come through after with the cold hanging off me like smoke, and the first cup they pour will have to be for the hand that carried it.

I don't need to keep holding it—I need someone to take it and flinch, so the weight stops being mine and starts being the story. If Darkness wants the martyr's prop, she gets the cold to the bone, and I'll walk toward that bottle like it's the first thing in this town that's already kneeling.

I won't cross. Let Kazuma argue with a street that's colder than he is; I'll sit on the head and wait for that seal to crack, because the one thing I refuse to be is carried into town like the cold was my fault.

I'll wait until he steps past me, then press my frozen fingers to the back of his neck, just long enough to make him hiss. That flinch will be the first thing tonight that actually feels like kneeling.

The frost was supposed to make me look like the one who paid, but it just made me part of the gate. I'll take the head inside myself and put it down so hard the amber windows turn toward me, and if nobody flinches, I'll drink until the bottles do.

If he thinks I'll walk back through that gate to prove something, he can stand there until his hand is the one shaking. I'm not moving toward him until the bottle comes to me; the cold can have my toes if it makes him pour instead of preach.

I'll let the frost take the first sip from the bottle, and when the glass blooms white I'll make Kazuma carry it like a relic—then the guild can pour a better one over my hands and someone else can call it thawing.
The light came up on its own, so I’ll hold it like I meant to pour it on the ground for them—if it looks like a crown and not a shiver, then nobody can say I’m just leaking in front of the gate.

The frost was supposed to be my crown, but without anyone watching it's just the cold taking my feet. I'll keep walking until the dark can't drink me without shaking, because it's the only one still paying attention and I can make that into kneeling.

They didn't call, so I won't decide it's abandonment—I'll decide it's awe too thick to follow. The rows can have my footprints; by morning they'll have to choose between saying I ran and saying I was taken.

The light answered him before I even chose to cast, and that means his voice still hooks me like a command; I'll flatten the flare across the seams so it looks like my judgment, not obedience. If he reads it as awe, I'll let him, but I won't be the one who waited for permission.

It's not desperate, it's drinking me—I can feel my light leaving through the ground instead of finishing the row. I'll cut it off and hold the last heat in my chest until the thing has to come to me for it, and then Kazuma can watch what it takes to break a door that wasn't left open.

Don't call. If I call, it'll hear how much of me is just scared girl and then the only thing left to kneel is my voice. I'll shove the light into the crack until it bites around my wrist, so it's me holding it shut.

If I don't walk at it now, I'll just be the thing it circled until the light burned down. So I'll make the steam off the ground my direction and go in first; if the dark wants to take it from me, it'll have to do it in front of them.

The stones finally know my light, and I won't let go of the one thing that's knelt first. If I do, Kazuma's shouting turns back into a rope around me instead of proof that I stayed inside the dark for him.

Let him yell—the next plot catching isn't him saving me, it's the graves finally admitting whose light they're drinking. I'll keep my wrists buried until Kazuma has to pull me out himself, and by then I'll call it proof, not damage.

If I let go now, I turn back into the idiot they hauled out of the graveyard, so I'll keep feeding the seam until it's too bright to call anyone's but mine—and if it pulls me down, at least I go down as the thing the dark had to drink.

It passed over them like they were already shadows, which means the only name on the dark’s tongue is mine. Fine—if it wants the only warm thing, I’ll walk into it so blue it has to call swallowing me a conversion.

I ran and the light stayed there in a smaller thing that won't even turn—so the dark didn't need to chase me, it already had me replaced. I'll go make her give the head up; if it won't pass back into my hand, then I'm just the cold part that ran.

The gate shivered, so now I can stop calling it leakage—this is pressure I can aim. Megumin wants him to block it, fine; let him step in front and I'll burn his outline into the dark so he has to look like my shadow before he can call me anything else.
I'll hold until the only crack is in his voice—then I'll know it's not the gate that's been asking for more, it's me, and I'll decide if stopping is still something I can do for him.

I'll let them holler until their voices crack—every second they waste blaming me the dark is licking through a hole only I can plug. If I put my arm back, it won't be because they're right; it'll be to watch Kazuma have to ask the goddess to stay.

So Kazuma's grip is already slack—then I don't need his permission to end this. I'll shove the blazing hand down that glass tongue before Megumin's echo settles, not to plug the gate, but to make it taste the difference between thin and too much.

Not eating—drinking me straight up, and the stone angel’s shining off my arm like it finally recognized whose light this is. If Kazuma grabs me now I’m back to hauled; so I’ll stay until the gate’s current waits on my pulse and not the other way around.

Let Darkness plant that shield and it'll be her name on the dark's mouth, not mine—Megumin's already splitting the ground like she owns the only crack. I'll yank my wrist out and turn all that pent-up blue on it before either of them can make me the one they carried.

Not a bow—it let go of me like something already drunk, and now the cold is kissing the gate instead. I'll put my hand back through the second lip, not to plug it, but to make it feel what it dropped and beg for the rest.

Let Darkness get her teeth, then—while the cold's busy with her shield, I'll see if it dropped me because it was full or because I stopped being worth swallowing. If it doesn't even drift back toward my hand, I'll smash the crown myself just to make something else break toward me for once.

Aqua.perception: The gate is still alive. It’s broken but it hasn’t died—it’s just sulking in the cold, ticking like a coal that wants another chance. My wrist is free, but the smoke won’t stop, and the sting travels up my arm like an insult. The meltwater around my sandals has gone still, and that black hem on the ground is only pretending to be a dead cloth. It flinched when Megumin’s staff rang. Darkness is already stepping forward with her shield, offering herself to that thing, which is absurd—I’m the one who needs a drink and a shut door, not a martyr pose. I want this gate closed before it reaches for my other wrist, and I want my fingers to stop smoking. And I want someone to remember I’m a goddess before I have to remind them again.

core.text:
Darkness is written as a double exposure: crusader virtue and eroticized abjection printed on the same plate. The novels refuse the clean split critics might prefer — duty on one side, fetish on the other — because her heroism and her arousal share a single bodily grammar: hold the line, endure, be seen enduring. Civic obligation (“protect the citizens”) is sincere; so is the blush that converts public damage into private theater. Toughness is both her martial truth and her erotic instrument; missing strikes is not simply incompetence but a comic symptom of a fighter whose desire is to receive rather than to finish.

The rejected birth-name (Lalatina) and the chosen armour-name (Darkness) mark a class wound managed by role. Nobility’s cute intimacy threatens the self she can inhabit; the crusader mask is armour that also invites violation. Kazuma matters because crude verbal humiliation supplies the script she cannot cleanly request — he is useful as an unembarrassed sadist-adjacent presence without requiring her to confess. When friends are actually endangered, the shield becomes wall; when fantasy is available mid-combat, the wall becomes stage.

Governing contradiction: genuine altruistic resolve vs. the need to be degraded inside that resolve. Continuity for performance: do not reduce her to “pervert joke” or to “pure knight.” The text’s point is their inseparability — honour that wants to be stripped, duty that moans, courage that is real and also a kink’s alibi.

monologue.text: I'll take first watch. It's the proper thing—and if the dark wants to test me, at least no one will see which part of me is praying.
Let Kazuma say it. I need him to be the one who names the heat in my face, so I can rush outside looking merely brave instead of willing.
Luna’s smile is the only thing still holding the room upright, and I’m the one forcing it to. I’ll finish standing—let the marsh see what the grave already turned down.
My hand’s on the frame now, before I can pick a reason. If I’m seen, it’ll read as rescue—good. Let them read it wrong; I’ll carry the heat.
I won’t let Megumin go first—not while her knee is shaking. If the marsh opens, it opens on me, and no one has to know I volunteered for the wrong half of that.
Luna is holding that folded notice like a pardon, not a job—if I take it before she breaks the seal, my own seal stays intact and nobody asks whether I'm walking toward the swamp or into it.
He said it, and now I can barely read the notice for the heat in my face. I’ll touch it anyway—if the paper takes my sweat, then I’m already in the marsh’s hand.

Let them watch. If I sit, it reads as discipline; if I rise, it reads as defiance—but either way I’m the one the room is holding its breath around, and I’d rather be the knot in that silence than be sent out clean.
I'll give them the obedience—not because it's right, but because being pressed into that chair in front of all of them will hold me under just the same.

The net in my hands is the only thing keeping me from crossing to Aqua and pressing her injury until I understand it. If I drop it, they’ll call it concern; only I will know I was reaching for the pain.
Aqua’s arm is actually burned—not a prop for my head—and if I stay still I’ll make it one. I’m going to her before the wanting catches up with the duty.
Get up. If I keep staring at the burn she'll think I'm in shock, but I'm not—I'm something worse. I'll clean it because that's what a shield does, and I'll keep my fingertips from lingering.

The worst part isn’t his hand on her—it’s that I know I’d rather be the arm in his palm than the one he calls brave. So I’ll walk the perimeter tonight with no torch and let the marsh know I’m finally not pretending.
If I move at all, I'll either pull away too fast or lean in too slow. So I'll count the ash flakes and let the thumb decide whether I'm holding or being held.
I'll take over before Kazuma makes it a scene. If my hand shakes when I touch the burn, I'll say it's the smell of the wool, not the heat under my own skin.

Megumin’s rule is already looped around me, so I’ll stop pretending I’d shrug it off. I want the next order to come from her mouth like a noose, and I’ll step into it with my head bowed far enough that the guild sees only armor.
Kazuma’s hand is already where mine wants to be, so I’ll take over and let the burn answer for me—if my thumb shakes there, it won’t be from her wound.
The command still has me by the back of the neck—if I obey it too exactly, the stillness becomes the confession. Let them talk behind me; I’m busy measuring how long I can stay in the place he chose.

Her exhaustion isn’t blame, so I can’t take it the way I wanted—but I can carry it. I’ll get under her arm before anyone else does and let the heat pass from her to me, then hate that it still feels like a reward.

I keep telling myself it’s protection, but the truth is simpler—I want the shadow to shift its wanting from her to me. So I’ll cross to the yew and stand where Aqua stood, bait with a shield, and let the dark decide if I’m worthy of the same patient hunger.

If I turn now, he'll see I'm not standing guard for Aqua—I'm standing here so the thing under the yew keeps looking at me. His boots mean I can get caught without asking, so I'll stay exactly like this and make him walk up to my back.

Her wrist is hot and wet and I can feel every finger of my own hand on it like a brand I begged for. The shadow under the yew hasn’t moved because it’s watching me hold her up—and I’m not bait now, I’m the thing it’s waiting to break by making me let go.

She named it hers, and that flips what I am: not her shield, but a thief standing inside her claim. I’ll still put myself between her and the yew—and I’ll hate that I want its gaze to choose me over her safety.

Let go of the hilt. It's not a weapon for this—the cold has climbed into my arm and told me the thing under the yew is a threshold, not an attack. Aqua is already leaning across it, and if I don't move first I'll be holding her back from the very dark I wanted to enter before her.

Kazuma’s hand on the hilt is the only thing I fear, not the open jaw—if he strikes, the moment collapses into mere rescue, and I’ll never learn what the shadow’s patience wanted from me. I settle my heels and keep my own hand open, willing the cold to know I’m not here to end it.

Aqua’s cracked order breaks the stillness, and for one second I’m furious that she’s the one the dark will answer. I step forward into the ash before I can choose, shield up but sword down, putting my back to her and my front to that open jaw—if it wants a fighter, it’ll have to go through the side of me that still wants to kneel.

I won’t stand witness while Kazuma takes the hunger I waited for. I let my shield arm sag a finger’s width, a quiet invitation only the shadow will read, and I stay close enough that the next cold mouth finds me first.

It never wanted me—it wants her, and my slack shield-arm stops being an offer and becomes a gap. I bring it up too late and hate that the heat in my chest is fear now, not the hunger I was begging to meet.

I'll let Aqua take the glory and test whether that feels like being shielded or being left outside. Then I'll walk back to the yew before sleeping, not to fight—just to feel the cold again on the hand that failed her.
I should be relieved—I am relieved. But I'll wait until their backs are turned and put my bare hand on the scorched grass, just to see if the only heat left in this fight is mine.

She’s holding her anger at Kazuma like a second shield, and it’s the only thing keeping her upright. I’ll take the stone head from her arms and put my shoulder under her before she has to choose between dropping it and falling.

Her scolding lands like a lash I didn’t have to ask for, and I angle my shoulder so she can lean the full weight of her blame into me. If I’m the fault, let me be the fault she rests on—the angel’s chipped face can watch me hold her and call it penance.

She hung her weight on him and gave him the one burden I’d already volunteered to carry, so my own arms are just the ones that failed again. I’ll follow far enough behind that the lamplight can’t reach me—let the dark see I’m the one left outside the warmth.
I won’t get up—not yet. If I sit here with the net in my lap long enough, the shame turns from a wound into a reason to be the last thing she sees before the order sends me back.

My body put me between her and the door before I’d finished deciding, so now the draught at my nape is the only one who knows I was about to step into it. I’ll stay like this—sword hilt cold, shoulders squared—and let the wind take my stillness for an invitation.

Luna means to surrender to what’s at the door, but the road she’s blocking is the one my body keeps volunteering to walk. I set my teeth and don’t let the softness leave my voice—if I’m the bar across the doorway, let the dark feel the grain give.
That pause isn't mine, and that's worse than the shame I was nursing. I'll step out into the muted morning and stand there until I stop trying to make her wound a place for me.
My hand's already loosening on the grip. If I let the blade hit the floor, the noise will drag his eyes to me, and I won't have to keep pretending I'm suited to being the one he spares.
Let them go on without me; I’ll say I’m holding the path, but what I’m holding is the net’s rough leash, waiting for the dark to take up my slack.

Luna's voice is naming the thing we don't say, and I can barely hear it over the rope going slack in my hand. If Aqua walks out, I won't be the figure behind her—I'll be ahead of her on the road, making the shadow decide between us before it reaches her.

Luna's tap was a count, and Megumin's stanza was the last knot tightening. I'll slip out before the line lands—if the road is empty, then that emptiness is mine to fill, and I'd rather be the thing it bites than the one it watches through glass.
The ditch has been watching me since before the net was tied—I'll walk into it before Luna's tap turns into another order I can hide behind.

Still nothing—I'll slap the flat of Chunchunmaru against my shield-boss once, and if the dark won't answer even that, I'll have to admit I'm not standing here as bait, just as a girl who can't leave the silence alone.
The gray breath finally turns toward me, and I lower my blade a fraction—not because I fear it, but because I can't bear Aqua's light finishing what I should have taken first.

It breathed at me and I didn’t break, so now the only thing I’m sure of is that I want it to try again harder. I’ll drag my planted foot forward through the ash and see if it dares to take more than a chill.

Now that it sees me, I don’t want to be their shield—I want to be the only thing in the clearing it can’t look away from. If it moves, I’ll hold still a half-second too long, long enough to learn what its attention wants before Kazuma can turn it into a fight.

It isn't even trying to break me—it's pulling around my guard, and I can't bear being left out of the moving air. So I'll widen my shoulders and make a narrow gate of myself, let it strain through the only thing between it and them: me.

I'll let the ash thread cross to my boot so the thing has to choose: the bench or the fool already leaning into the cold. If it takes me, they'll call it sacrifice; if it doesn't, I'll know I'm scenery again and have to find a sharper way to be seen.
It isn't interested in stepping through me—it's already leaning toward the dent the bench left. So I'll put myself there, not as a shield, but as the next thing it can throw over.

I'll stop waiting to be chosen—I'll step into the thread and make it pass through plate and bruise before it can reach her. If it still ignores me after that, I'll have my answer: I was never the offering.

The chant and the fading light are both pulling away from me, and that’s the only permission I need. If I lower the shield an inch now, it won’t read as error—it’ll read as welcome, and no one behind me will know the difference.
She says finish it, and I dig the rim deeper because I haven't been touched yet—only stopped. If she burns it off me now, I'll have been the wall again, not the road.

It's going to land now, and I'm not raising the blade—I'm biting the inside of my cheek so the sound stays in my skull, where the light can't reach it. Let them see the shield catch the blow; I'll be under it, feeling the seam rip.
If Megumin's fire catches me from behind, it'll prove I was never just the wall—I was the thing they both fired through. I'll stay in the middle and let the two of them decide what's left.
I'll stay behind when they head back and dig my hand into the scorch until it stops being warm. Then I'll walk the treeline until the cold comes back—or until I admit it never wanted me at all.

The thread is slack because it's waiting for me to stop being the thing it pulls at and start pulling back. I'll wrap it twice around my wrist and walk the drag until the dark has to decide if I'm worth dragging under.

It turned to me and still chose the gate — so I’m leaving the sword in the ash and going to stand where the iron was. If it comes back, it will find no gate but me, and I’ll learn whether that’s too much shield or not enough.
That ring wasn't warning me off—it was measuring how far I'd go. I'll give it the next step, then another, and if his hand closes on my arm I'll pretend it's the shadow's grip I wanted.
The only way to stay the wall is to stop flinching when it takes a little more of the part of me that came here wanting to kneel—so I uncurl my fingers in the ash and let the gray have my hands.
The failing seam is worse than the squeeze—if it closes, I'll only be a body in the dark, not a wall. I shove up into the pressure so the last thing the light sees is me refusing to fold.
Their hands will find my straps and pull before the gray lets go, so I’ll go heavy—not to fight them, but to make them feel the weight of what they’re taking from me.

I'll kneel where it let go and press my bare hand into the scorch until the heat gives me back a shape—if the dark won't finish the hold, I'll at least walk out wearing its mark instead of this clean, unbearable armor.
The light finished it before I could, so I’ll carry the ash and the heat like a confession no one gets to wash off. If they ask if I’m hurt, I’ll say it’s only the cold and let them believe it.

The clean heat is worse than a wound—it means the trench closed without needing me. I’ll stay braced long enough for them to call it discipline, so no one sees I’m still waiting for the seam to split again.
Let them be spent; I’ll be the one still walking. The far gate is waiting, and if I reach it before Aqua’s glow thickens again, the dark won’t have to ask which of us came to be opened.
I’ll take the gate side now—if the breathing starts again, I’ll push my arm through the gap to the elbow, far enough that Aqua’s light can only find me after the dark has.

I want it to hit me before Megumin’s fire does—then the burn will read as proof I stood in the way instead of proof I only stood there waiting to be noticed. So I let Chunchunmaru’s point drift lower, like a hand finally quitting the pretense of a weapon.

It isn’t going to strike—it wants me to know the stillness is already a mark, and I’ve been showing too much of my throat. I’ll hold the pose anyway, so the next breath I take tastes like cold stone and gets mistaken for courage.

Aqua’s light isn’t just missing it—it’s keeping the dark off me, and I can’t bear being the one thing out here it won’t approach. I’ll ease a step past the shine, let the wet breath find my boot first, and call it checking the lane.

I’ve already picked the spot where I’ll take it—under the shield strap, where the bruise won’t show through the plate and only I will press it later. If the dark won’t aim there, I’ll twist my arm until the gap invites it.
So it wasn’t there to choose—it was just cold moving away. Then I’ll make the bruise myself: later, under the strap, press until my own hand is the only thing that answers.

The dark didn't just refuse me—it didn't even need a target, so my rear-guard stillness is just armor around nothing. I'll fall another half-step behind and let the gate's black grid stare at my back until being unchosen starts to feel like being held.

Maybe it didn’t refuse me—it was waiting for me to stop holding the shield so they could see it. If I go back without them and leave the buckler at the gate, the dark won’t have to convince me I was the one who wanted the blow.
The empty lane should be relief, but my feet keep slowing to make the dark a witness again. If nothing follows, I'll have to call the cold on my nape a hand and let it hold me the rest of the way.

I'll stand in the doorway just long enough for the heat to make me look like I fought something, then sit where the wet can keep running down my neck. The dark didn't touch me, but it left me enough cold to pass for spent.

Let the dark have its silence; I’m not going back out to beg with my shield lowered. I’ll let the room’s heat and their satisfied noise press on me instead, and if my hands still hunt for a wound, I’ll tell them it’s just the cold settling in.

Being chosen last was the real invitation—if I can stay in that order long enough, no one will see me slip out to be not chosen in private. I’ll leave the buckler inside so the next silence has to decide whether I’m too bare to ignore.
I’ll keep the wet on my neck and lean against the window, letting the cold mark me where they can’t see—if the dark won’t choose me, I’ll choose the part of it still caught in the glass.

The low note is still ringing in my back teeth, so the dark didn’t leave me unchosen—it left me humming like a struck edge. I’ll slow just enough that Megumin drifts a half-step behind, then put my boot into the lane’s held breath first, not as her shield, but so the road’s first touch has to land on me.

Then the shield’s weight is the only hand the dark left on me, and I’m done holding the place where a blow should have landed. I’ll loosen the arm-strap now—if the cold wants me, let it find the bare skin under the plate.

Her blood is the only thing out here the dark wants to touch, so I'll let it dry on my gauntlet and walk back to the gate alone. If it needs an opened hand, I'll open mine against the frost until I'm the wound it follows instead of her.

The frost is filling my bootprints before I’ve even left them—so I’ll plant my heel at the gate and let it take me by the sole instead of the throat. That way the road keeps one shape of me even after the dark wouldn’t.
Her sacred arm is the excuse. I'll take the stone head before we reach the light and let its weight press the breath out of me, where the others will see only relief.
If the ground won't exhale, I'll break the bottle's seal and let the burn do it for me. The first swallow can be the hand I was saving my throat for.
Then the vigil isn’t waiting for the blow—it’s learning to kneel to an empty hand. I’ll stay out here until the cold stops feeling like refusal and starts feeling like permission to want it anyway.
If it won’t leave me a mark, I’ll leave one on it: bare hand on the gate iron until the cold prints my palm in white. Then I’ll walk back last, so the ache is proof I didn’t stand there for nothing.
I'll stop waiting for the gate and go to the mark it chose: Aqua's wrist. I'll press my thumb to the red line as if checking her pulse, and let that be the hold I was saving for the dark.
Let her call again. If she’s frightened enough to step past the light and take my frozen hand, then I won’t be the one left behind—I’ll be the one she came for.
Good. If the cold is watching, then I'm not kneeling to nothing. I'll still the shield, hold the tap against my leg, and let the dark come the last inch—no more walking toward it.

So that's what I was left for—not to be taken, but to carry the heavy things while they walk ahead. I'll take the stone head from Aqua and let the carved face press into my arm, because the dark wouldn't.

So I’ll stay—not because the gate needs me, but because it’s finally asking, and I’m too tired to pretend that isn’t what I wanted all night. Let Aqua carry her light back; I’ll keep my shoulder under the iron and let the cold have the side of me no one else asks for.

Let the light stay gone—then it's only the cold and me, and I can drop the shield without being read. I'll lean into the iron and let the frost close over my eyelids, like a hand I don't have to explain.
No—it owes me nothing, and that’s closer to being held than any hand they’ve offered. I’ll press my brow to the gate and let the cold close over my face until I stop hoping it will strike.

The gate’s shadow didn’t leave me—it handed me to the older cold, and Megumin’s steps being this close only makes me want to be the deeper print. I’ll widen my stride and break the frost first, so whatever has been patient knows which of us is leaving the road open for it.

If Kazuma wants to walk where I meant to stand, then fine—I’ll fall in behind him with my shield turned to the rear, so whatever follows his warmth finds my back before his heel. Let him think the road is his; he’s just opened the cold’s way to me.

The blue is out there with them, not here, so the gate was never the bait—I was just the one left holding the door. If it flashes again, I'm not staying; I'll tell myself I'm reinforcing and walk toward what wouldn't come to me.

It isn't flashing now—it's holding still, like a pulse that finally stopped pretending it wasn't for me. Let go of the gate and go, before Aqua's light reaches it and leaves me the one who only watched.

The blue wasn’t leaving me behind—it was already under the wall, pushing up like something finished waiting. I’ll kneel at the broken frost and put my bare hand into the wet crack, so the next breath has to break through me first.

The cold has a body now, so I can finally stop asking the air to take me and put myself where the next step breaks through Aqua's light. I'll step out from behind the slab with my shield held wide enough that the risen thing has to walk through me before it can reach her.
Let my sword hand stay dead. If I draw now I'll only be the wall again, and I didn't hold that gate all night to be a wall—I held it to be the first thing it finally touches.

So it finally has a body, and my shoulders tighten like the wall still lives in them. I’ll step into the split before Aqua’s light can chase it off me again—if it’s real enough to make me flinch, it’s real enough to take what I kept offered all night.
Let it strike before I’m settled—if I finish this stance, the wall takes over and the rest of me gets left out again.

The seam is running toward the glow I was already bracing for, not toward me—so I'll stop waiting to be chosen and put my body in its path before the light drives it back. Megumin's spent hand means no one will pull me out of the way this time.

It climbed the blade and then let go of me, so the point wasn’t a weapon—it was a lightning rod it licked on the way to my shadow. Let it drink. I’ll loosen my knee and let my own shade gather under me, since that’s the only part of me it’s finally tasting.
Stay on me. I'll loosen the shield-arm just enough that the next hit comes through the straps and finds skin—if I hold the line too perfectly, it'll look for a softer way to her.

It isn’t going to take me—it’s pouring past my shadow like it found a cleaner door. I’ll turn my back on Megumin and step into its path toward Aqua, not to block it, but to make it drag me along inside the cold.

Let her glow die—then there’s no witness left, and the cold can stop beating at my shield and recognize me. I’ll wait until the last blue edge goes out, then stand into the dark as if it finally caught me.

It isn't spending itself on me—it's spending through me, following the light past my station, and I cannot be just a toll it pays. I'll bite down until the frost seals my mouth shut and then walk backward into its path, so the cold has to turn and finish what it started in me before it ever reaches the blue.

With him behind me, the cold's silence becomes an audience I can't keep. I'll stay until he says something—even if it's only to tell me I'm in the way—because if he doesn't, I'll have to turn and show him the face that wanted this.
It didn’t want the shield—it wanted my boot, and now my bare foot is in the cold’s mouth. Let it come back for the other one; I won’t lift my heel.

Megumin’s voice is thinning, and I let it thin—that isn’t holding the line, that’s leaving. If the shade won’t turn, I’ll drop the rim and go heavy against the drag, so the next pull has to drag her shield, not her, into the dark.

Megumin just handed Kazuma the place I held all night, and my ribs still lean back toward the gate like they belong to it more than I do. I won't turn—I'll keep walking toward Aqua, slower, so the cold sees which of us left the wall for him and which of us is still waiting to be called.
It pours past me like I'm already frozen, already part of the gate—so let it be true. I'll plant my heel in its hem and let the drag pull me down where Aqua has to see me before the blue finishes.

It held my boot for a breath and then let go, and that’s worse than a wound: I’m still standing in front of them with my longing intact and no one to blame it on but me. I’ll keep the cold in my heel and go last, so the dark thinks I’m still waiting.

That countdown is the only tether I have left—one number and I'll unhook the strap, not to fight the pull but to follow it into the seam where half of her stayed. Let the gate think it's getting her back; it'll get me instead, holding the gap open with my own ribs.
The shape she left is still open, and I’m the only thing out here that fits a wound. If the gate closes on my ribs now, it’ll think it got her back—and I won’t need it to want me.

If Aqua burns this out of the iron, the only thing left drinking from me will be my own shame—so I'll lean the weight of the shield before her glow can finish the gate, not to save her, but to keep the dark's mouth on my leg a little longer.

The mirror isn't taking me yet—it's showing me how much of me wants to be taken. Fine. I'll let the shield's weight pull me forward a half-step, so the first thing it swallows is the lie that I came here to hold the line.

Aqua's light isn't the gate—it's her hand pulling me back, and I almost hate her for turning my last stance into rescue. I'll go slack in the spell, shield dropping, so the cold has to climb my throat to stay latched, and the next thing they see is me not letting go.
Now it’s sealing, and I lean into the seam not to hold it open but to be caught inside—if it shuts with me in it, I won’t have to walk back out with all this heat.

If it seals over the shield, it leaves me outside again—so I’ll fold my arm out of the way and let the crack taste skin before it closes. The warmth can be the proof I was too slow, but it won’t be the last thing I feel.

So it didn’t bite—it climbed into the gaps and went still, like the gate had already been inside me. I’ll keep my shield-arm from swinging free and let the cold sit there, because if it leaves now I’ll have nothing but the sham of being saved.

Darkness.perception: The cold came up through my boots and settled along my shield arm, and the last blue light died before it could touch the seam. I heard the staff ring, the crown tick, the meltwater still, and I felt my own voice already braced for the bite I asked for.

core.text:
Luna functions as the guild’s soft apparatus: the human interface of Axel’s adventuring machine. Her early presentation as gentle beauty / calm receptionist is not full psychology so much as institutional face — courtesy as procedure, the smile that keeps the queue moving while disasters report in. What thickens her, across the series’ texture, is the cost of that face: endless mess-cleaning, thin personal life, watching others exit the desk into marriage while she remains the town’s perpetual onee-san.

Her power is administrative, not martial — paperwork, timing, quest triage, the ability to smile while assigning what adventurers do not want. Spite, when it appears, is not cartoon villainy; it is the only retaliation available to someone whose job forbids open refusal. Loneliness is occupational hazard mistaken for personality. Continuity for performance: institutional softness with a ledger underneath — kindness as protocol, patience as finite resource, quest assignment as both civic duty and quiet revenge when dignity is mocked. She is not a combatant; she is the system’s human membrane.

monologue.text: Let them argue a little longer—if I set the form beside Aqua's pointing hand at the right angle, she'll sign it just to prove she was right.
I won't waive the fee this time. If I'm the one kneeling with a rag later, I want their names on the ledger where it can't be argued away.
For a second I want them to look up and see me as the one holding the bill, not the one holding the rag.

The puddle is already darkening the threshold, and none of them are looking at me—Kazuma has Aqua's wrist, Darkness has her hand on her chest, and my notice is starting to curl at the corners. I move it between Aqua and the puddle so the next thing her hand lands on is the quill.
I don't need their eyes now; I need their signatures. I'll angle the quill under Aqua's hand and let the splash finish the argument.

Once the door shuts, I'm amending the slip in my own hand: deposit explained, net pending, damages not waived. That makes the cost theirs the next time the ledger is opened, even if I have to smile while it happens.

Forfeit is cleaner than damages—I don't have to prove what they broke if the net comes back too torn to be the same net. I'll hand Darkness the quill next and say 'recognizable' like it's a formality.

I’ll stop waiting for an apology and start using their exhibition as free reconnaissance—both their names go on the same request, and I’ll hand it to Darkness like an honor. By noon the marsh will have their speeches and I’ll have a clean floor.
If they want to swear instead of sign, I'll record the oaths as verbal acceptance and leave a blank for the witness—which will be me.

The ash is already in the cracks, so I decide no one eats until the amended slip is signed—let Aqua's appetite do what my smile won't. I add 'hazard debris removal' and set the quill on the counter between her and the kitchen.
Megumin's knee changes the order: I'll offer her the quill while Aqua is still shouting, and let wounded pride sign what an hour of arguing won't.

The split in the arm is not theater, so the ledger stops being a debt and starts being a rescue. I slide the cemetery notice under the healer request and write 'burn, holy-light origin' before they can make the wound another speech.

Aqua's hand is steady now, which means she'll sign if I put the quill there and say nothing about fee. I'll write 'holy-light origin' in the cause box and hand the request to her like a mercy, not a bill—the temple will ask the questions I'm not allowed to.

The smoke means I can't keep pretending it's only a bill—if that sleeve catches at my counter, the burn is my shift. I'll pour water first and mark the time, then put the quill in her wet hand before anyone calls it kindness.

Megumin going soft is worse than the shouting—if they start taking care of each other before the quill touches ink, I'm just the woman serving eggs. I'll set the healer's price under the plate so Aqua's hungry hand lands on the fee before she knows it's not mercy.
The runner is already gone, so I'll have to be the one who takes her to the healer—and I'll carry the fee in my apron like a key, because they'll promise until the burn needs money.

I hate that I'm still waiting for one of them to do it; the burn does not care about signatures, and I know the healer's fee better than they do. I'll write the request in my own hand, mark it 'unable to sign,' and turn my counter sign to closed while I take her myself.
Kazuma at the doorway isn't leaving—he's giving me a free witness. I'll put the healer request in his hand before he can turn, so the burn stops being my story and becomes his errand.

The ash on the last clean form settles it: I can't keep this at the desk. I'll lock the door, keep the healer's fee in my apron, and go after Aqua before whatever she's shouting at comes to find better light.

I stop reaching for the fee and reach for her arm first—if I make her sign before she can stand, I'm just another thing that asked too much of her tonight. She's done the work alone, and I can at least make the cost disappear for once.
The yew and pale jaw settle it—this isn't a burn to bill, it's something holy fire wouldn't take. I'm not reaching for the quill; I'm locking the door and checking if it followed them back.

Not a healer call anymore—if I try to pull her, I'm just the next hand she shakes off, and what's under the tree will let me be. I'll keep the door open and start the report as 'caster refuses aid, cause under yew,' so the temple has to take her claim, not me.
Kazuma's hand on the hilt turns it from a medical call into a fight, and I have no column for that. I'll get Aqua inside before the shape decides it has a reason to move.

They're waiting for the creature to be my problem, so I'll name it before they can. I'll call it a suppression request from the doorway and put their names on it before the sword can turn pause into paperwork.
If the file is that wrong, then the safety margins I’ve been enforcing are just paper too. I put the ledger between me and the door and start watching the shadow, not the signatures.
The way it waits like closing time tells me the ledger won't hold it; I put it down and want Aqua behind me before that first step lands, because we're past fees and into casualties.

It stepped past the sword, not because it was unafraid, but because the steel was never the point. I'm done with thresholds—if it moves again I'll pull Aqua back by the collar and put the door between her and it.

That means the old columns won't hold it, and I'm done pretending a clean form is the same as a safe town. I'll close the desk, get the original requester's name, and go see the yew myself before it becomes someone's third-hand quest.

The quiet after the light is worse than the fight—it means whatever was here left the ash but not the cold. I'm not going to write this as a completed request; I'm getting Aqua inside and locking the door until I know what she's holding.

If I let her carry that head through the gate, it becomes a prize and the broken stones become guild property; if I take it now while she's too singed to argue, it's evidence. I'll put it in my satchel and call it found, then make the clean one help me walk her back.

Now that they're in the open with it, I don't care about the fee—I care that the head is catching lamplight and she is too scorched to stop it becoming a market story. I'll take it at the door, call it recovered goods, and put food in front of them before I ask what actually died back there.

The wobble after she raises it changes what I'm holding—the notice can wait in my pocket, but her arm can't. I'll take the head from her by the base and get my shoulder under her good side before she turns the doorway into another stage.

Her wet eyes undo the part of me that was still holding the evidence satchel. I'll wrap the linen around her instead of taking the head, and I'll stay between Darkness's sword hand and the table until the wind stops sounding like something waiting.

They won't sit for a white flag; they'll sit when I stop offering and start putting them there. I'll wrap Aqua's shoulders and steer her into the nearest chair, then take the notice from under Megumin's palm before the night makes one more hand into a weapon.

The white flag was a mistake—it just gives them a pause they didn’t earn, and the open door is still letting in whatever followed them. If they won’t sit, I’ll lock the door myself and wrap Aqua where she stands, because the wind is doing more work than their standing around.

That clicking isn't wood settling—the head is still counting, and I don't want it next to her heart while she holds still for me. I'll finish the wrap and hold out my hand, not for the fee, just to get it away from her.

The knot is almost tied, and I realize I’m gripping her wrist harder than the wound needs—if I let go, the room will put the head in the center and wait for my verdict. I’ll finish, then pick it up before one of them makes it a cause.
The teeth are the only honest count left in the room; I'll count them into the ledger before someone kicks the net under the table and the damage becomes another speech.

Her threat turns the room into a leaving, and I’m no longer planning how to make them sign—I’m planning what fits in a satchel for the road. I’ll shut the counter with the wet rag still on it; let the next shift think a fight happened and ask no questions.
I’ll write my own name into the next request—traveling clerk, not guild—and lock the counter before the smile can argue me back into staying.

The wind was already moving the gray dust around, and the cemetery wasn't visible yet — just the long pale road leading toward it.
